beats.text: Four hundred eighteen million dollars. That is what the real
estate industry agreed to pay after buyers sued over how commissions
worked. Every headline said the same thing. This
ends six percent commission forever. It did not.
There is also a new piece of paper you are now required to sign before
an agent will even show you a house. Most
buyers sign it in the car, in the driveway, without reading it. I
would bet real money you do not know what is actually in it. I
will show you exactly what to check, before we are done here. Here
is why this catches people off guard. The lawsuit
was real. The settlement was real. Four
hundred eighteen million dollars is not a small number. So
everyone assumed the price of using an agent must have dropped along with
it. Most buyers now walk in expecting one of
two things. Either commissions collapsed. Or
they now have to pay their agent directly, out of pocket, like
a lawyer. Neither of those is quite true. And
the part that should actually worry you has nothing to do with the percentage.
It is a contract. One you now have to sign before
you even walk through a door with an agent. It can lock
you into that specific agent, at that specific rate, for
weeks or months. That promise can hold whether
or not you end up buying anything through them at all. Most
buyers sign it without reading what it actually promises. Not
because they are careless. Because nobody told them
this piece of paper was new, or that it was negotiable at all. So
let's separate what changed from what did not. The
lawsuit itself was brought by home sellers, arguing the industry's
own rules had quietly kept commissions inflated for decades.
It became one of the largest antitrust cases real estate has
ever seen, and it did not target one bad broker. It
targeted the entire system's default setting. So,
the old system. For decades, a home sale
typically carried one combined commission, historically around
six percent of the price. The seller paid it.
Both halves. Their own agent's half, and the
buyer's agent's half, baked into the listing before a buyer
ever saw the house. The buyer never saw that number.
It just lived inside the price. The lawsuit's
core argument was simple. Buyers had no easy
way to see, or negotiate, what their own agent was actually
being paid. That blind spot, the plaintiffs
argued, quietly pushed commissions higher than they needed to be,
year after year. The lawsuit targeted exactly
that setup. And it produced two real rule changes,
effective August of 2024. One.
A listing can no longer advertise what it will pay a buyer's agent.
That number is off the public listing site entirely. Two.
Before an agent can tour homes with you, you now have to sign a written
agreement. It states, in writing, what
you are agreeing to pay that agent, and for how long that promise
holds. That second one is the part almost
nobody explains. It is also brand new. Before
August of 2024, most buyers never signed anything
like it before their first showing. Now, the
number everyone actually cares about. Did the
price drop? Per Bankrate, agents typically
earn between two and a half and three percent each in today's market. And
per a 2026 survey of real estate agents, the national
average total commission now sits at five
point seven percent. Six percent, to five point seven. That
is the entire headline change. Here is the gap
that actually matters. In that same survey,
thirty eight percent of recent sellers still believed six percent was
the standard. Only fourteen percent of them actually
paid a full six. The belief outlasted the reality
by years. So who pays the buyer's agent now,
if it is not automatically baked in? Mostly,
still the seller. Per reporting on life after the
settlement, many sellers keep covering it voluntarily, because
refusing to can scare buyers away from the listing. The
out-of-pocket buyer is the exception right now. Not
the new rule. Think of it like a restaurant quietly
moving from "tip included" to "please tip your server" on the receipt.
Most customers still tip about the same amount. The
money just became visible instead of automatic. But
here is the real catch, if you do end up owing it yourself. On
most loan types, including FHA and conventional loans,
that fee generally cannot be rolled into your mortgage. It
is treated as a separate cost, paid in cash, at closing.
Let's make that concrete. Say you are buying a four
hundred thousand dollar house, and you owe your agent two point
eight percent yourself. That is about eleven thousand
two hundred dollars. In cash. On
top of your down payment and your closing costs. For
comparison, at the old six percent split, the buyer's
half on that same house would have run twelve thousand dollars. The
dollar amount barely moved. What moved is whether
you can see it coming. Say that number out loud to
yourself before you assume the lawsuit made buying cheaper. Digging
past the headline and into the actual paperwork is the whole point
of this channel. If that is useful to you, subscribing
means the next one finds you before your own closing does. Now
the honest part. First, commission has always
been negotiable, in every state, both before this settlement
and after it. Nothing here is a fixed government rate.
Treat every number in this video as an average, not your quote. Your
local market matters too. A hot market with
multiple offers gives you far less leverage to negotiate than a slow
one where a seller is eager to close. That is true
on both sides of the table. A seller in a slow
market has more reason to cover your agent's fee just to keep your offer
competitive. A seller with five offers already
on the table has almost none. Second, the four
hundred thousand dollar example is my own math, built from Bankrate's
published rate. It is a real, verified percentage
applied to a round number. It is not a quote from
one specific sale. Third, the loan-financing
rule has some uncertainty. As of the sources I could

about how the industry works, not legal or financial advice
for your specific purchase. Buyer-broker agreements
vary by brokerage and by state. This channel
has nothing to sell you, and no referral fee riding on which
agent, or which agreement, you sign. The
point here is not to make you distrust every agent on sight. Most
are not trying to hide anything from you. The point
is that you read your own agreement with real questions in mind, because
the paperwork changed faster than anyone explained it. Agents
did not write these new rules either. They are adjusting
to them in real time, same as buyers. So
here is exactly what to do. Five things, before
you ever tour a house. One. Ask
for the buyer-broker agreement before the day you meet an agent. Not
while you are standing in the driveway with a pen already in your hand. Read
the number. Read how long the agreement locks you in.
Read whether it is exclusive to that one agent, or whether you can
still work with someone else. All three lines are
negotiable, not fixed print. Two. Ask
directly if that percentage is negotiable. It legally
always has been, before this settlement and after it. Asking
is not rude, and it does not insult the agent. It
is the entire point of the new paperwork existing in the first place.
Three. Get the agreement in writing before you commit
to one agent exclusively. An open, non-exclusive
arrangement lets you work with more than one agent while you're still deciding
who fits. Once you sign exclusive, that option
is gone. Four. When you make
an offer, you can ask the seller to cover your agent's fee as part
of the deal. Many sellers still say yes. In
a lot of markets, it barely changes the math for them, because
it used to be baked into the price they were already accepting. It
costs you nothing to ask. It is a normal line
in a normal offer, not an awkward favor. Five.
If there is any chance you will owe it yourself, set that cash aside
separately from your down payment. Do not assume it rides
along inside your mortgage. For most loans,
it does not. Treat it like a fourth cost, sitting
next to your down payment, your closing costs, and your moving
budget. Not a rounding error hiding inside one
of them. So, quickly, what actually changed
and what did not. The rule changed. No
more commission listed publicly, and a signed agreement required
before you tour. The number barely moved: six
percent down to five point seven. And the belief

pay it. The four hundred eighteen million dollar
lawsuit did not make buying a house cheaper. It
made the price visible, on paper, in a contract, before
you tour a single house. For decades, that
number was invisible by design. Now it has your
name and your signature on it. What you do with that
